notes:
These are verse-by-verse notes on Numbers 18. Each point gives its source page. Some verses have more coverage than others, and I've said at the end what I couldn't find.

## 1. Verse-by-verse: the traditional reading

**v. 1**
- Gill says "father's house" means the Levites, while "you and your sons" means the priests. He says Aaron's family had to be answerable for my sins, errors, and mistakes that should be committed by them in the discharge of their office. This shows the priesthood was a burden, not something to envy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-18.html
- Ellicott says "the iniquity of the sanctuary" covered sins that defiled it. It also covered defilement by the imperfections connected with the services of the priests and the offerings of the people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-18.html
- Guzik (Enduring Word) says this was the flip side of the honour Aaron received in Numbers 17. God never gives authority without accountability; the two always go together. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-18/
- Precept Austin's study note says the verse balanced Aaron's high honour. It was meant to calm the people's fears and ease their envy: the priest would be blamed for anything done wrongly in the sanctuary. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-18-commentary

**v. 2**
- Ellicott says "joined" plays on the name Levi. The Hebrew verb is the same one Leah used when she named him (Genesis 29:34). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-18.html
- Gill says the Levites were brought only into the court of the Tabernacle. They helped kill and skin the sacrifices and catch the blood. Calling them Aaron's "brothers" may have been meant to make them content with his priesthood. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-18.html
- Ellicott says the Levites served in the court, while the priests served in both the court and the holy place. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-18.html
- Guzik notes the Levites are described as serving three parties: the priests, the people (Numbers 16:9) and God (Deuteronomy 10:8). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-18/

**v. 3**
- Gill says that if Levites touched the holy things, both groups would die. The priests would die for allowing it and the Levites for pushing in. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-18.html
- Precept Austin draws the same point: the priests were responsible for keeping the Levites away from the holy furnishings. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-18-commentary
- Guzik gives Korah as the example of a Levite who came too near and died. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-18/

**v. 4**
- Gill reads "outsider" as anyone from the other tribes. He notes Jewish writers take it as anyone who wasn't a priest. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-18.html
- Guzik quotes Allen: here "stranger" means everyone except the Levites working under the priests. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-18/

**v. 5**
- Guzik says that if the Levites must not covet the priests' work, the priests must not neglect it either. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-18/
- Jensen (quoted on Precept Austin) says any atonement only worked if the priests did their duties faithfully. Their ultimate aim was that wrath would not come on Israel again. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-18-commentary

**v. 6**
- Matthew Henry says the Levites were given to the priests as a gift. We are to value it as a great gift of the divine bounty to have those joined to us that will be helpful and serviceable to us in the service of God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_018.cfm
- Wiersbe (on Precept Austin) compares the Levites to the seven men of Acts 6, who freed the apostles for other work. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-18-commentary

**v. 7**
- Ellicott says the "veil" here is the inner curtain in front of the Most Holy Place. The Hebrew word (*parocheth*) is used only of that second curtain. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-18.html
- Guzik quotes Morgan: the priesthood was a gift, entirely of grace and not earned. He quotes Allen that the Levites were never "priests in training". https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-18/
- Precept Austin connects this to Numbers 17:12–13, where the people feared they would all die. God's answer was a priest who could come near on their behalf. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-18-commentary

**v. 8**
- Gill says the priests received these offerings "because of the anointing", that is, because of their consecrated office. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-18.html
- Guzik quotes Allen: something was holy because it had been given to the Lord for his use, not because of some mysterious quality inside it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-18/

**v. 9**
- Ellicott says "the fire" is the fire on the altar of burnt offering. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-18.html
- Gill explains the Jewish distinction between "most holy" offerings and "lighter" holy offerings. The priests got the parts of sacrifices not burned on the altar. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-18.html

**v. 10**
- Ellicott says only priests and the males of their families could eat these. They had to eat them in the Tabernacle court (Leviticus 6:16, 26; 7:6). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-18.html

**v. 11**
- Gill says these lesser holy gifts could be eaten at home by the priest's family and by slaves bought or born in the house. Hired servants and guests could not eat them. "Clean" means ceremonially clean, for example not having touched a dead body. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-18.html
- Ellicott points to Leviticus 22:10–13 for these rules. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-18.html

**vv. 12–13**
- Gill says "best" is literally "fat", the best part of anything. The firstfruits were brought in a basket to the sanctuary (Deuteronomy 26:2). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-18.html

**v. 14**
- Gill: anything devoted to the Lord outright (fields, houses, cattle) went to the priests. Things devoted for a set purpose, such as temple repairs, went to that purpose (Leviticus 27). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-18.html

**vv. 15–16**
- Guzik says the firstborn son was never to be sacrificed. God did not want human sacrifice of any kind, so a payment was made instead. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-18/
- Ellicott notes that five shekels was also the price paid for firstborn sons who had no Levite to stand in for them (Numbers 3:47). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-18.html
- Gill says the time and price were fixed, yet the text still says "according to your valuation" (compare Leviticus 27:5). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-18.html

**vv. 17–18**
- Gill says the priests took the animals themselves rather than money. Jewish writers held that firstling meat could be eaten over two days and a night, like the breast and thigh of the peace offering. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-18.html
- Ellicott points out a difficulty. Deuteronomy 12:17–18 has the owners eat the firstlings. So either the law was later changed, or v. 18 limits the priests' share to the breast and right leg. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-18.html

**v. 19 ("covenant of salt")**
- Ellicott says it means a covenant that cannot be broken. He notes the Greeks asked "Where is the salt?" when someone broke an agreement. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-18.html
- Gill says it is unbreakable and lasting, but only until the gospel age came and for as long as Aaron's priesthood lasted. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-18.html
- Guzik says salt stands for purity, for lasting (it preserves) and for value (it was costly). He quotes Spurgeon that the covenant could not change or decay. He also mentions an old custom: once you had eaten a man's salt, you were his friend for life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-18/

**v. 20**
- Ellicott says Aaron speaks for the whole priesthood here; he himself never entered Canaan. He applies the verse to Christians: everyone in Christ's royal priesthood has God as their portion, in life, in death and forever. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-18.html
- Gill gives the reason for having no land: the Levites would not be tied up with worldly business or farming, but could give themselves fully to God's service. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-18.html
- Guzik links the verse to Psalms 16:5, 73:26 and 142:5. Since all believers are a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9), all have the Lord as their portion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-18/

**v. 21**
- Ellicott says this is the "first tithe", a tenth of all the land's produce. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-18.html
- Guzik says the tithe was wages for work, not a gift. It belonged first to God, so failing to tithe robbed God, not the Levite (Malachi 3:8–10). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-18/
- Jamieson, Fausset & Brown say having no land kept the Levites free for service and built a bond between them and the people. It also spread them through the tribes as teachers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Num/Num_018.cfm

**v. 22**
- Ellicott says "bear sin" first means bringing guilt on yourself and suffering for it. The later meaning, bearing sin to atone for it, grows out of that. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-18.html
- Gill: intruding into the priest's office was punishable by death. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-18.html

**v. 23**
- Jamieson, Fausset & Brown say the Levites would bear the penalty if they guarded the holy things carelessly. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Num/Num_018.cfm
- Guzik: if they lived on the tithe, they had to do the job, and do it diligently. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-18/

**v. 24**
- Gill says the Levites held the tithe from God, not from the people. It was as much their rightful inheritance as land was for the other tribes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-18.html

**vv. 25–26**
- Ellicott says this part goes to Moses rather than Aaron, because Aaron's family was directly involved. A better translation is "a tithe of the tithe." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-18.html
- Matthew Henry says the Levites were God's tenants and owed him rent. Thus now, ministers must be charitable out of what they receive. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_018.cfm
- Guzik: even people supported by God's people must learn to give. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-18/

**v. 27**
- Gill (quoted in the Preacher's Homiletical) says the Levites' gift was as acceptable to God as if it came from their own fields and winepresses. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/numbers-18.html
- Ellicott says the Hebrew word for the winepress's "fulness" means fully ripe grain or wine. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-18.html

**vv. 28–29**
- Jamieson, Fausset & Brown say the best of the Levites' tithes had to go to the priests. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Num/Num_018.cfm

**vv. 30–31**
- Ellicott says that once the priests' tenth was paid, the rest belonged to the Levites as ordinary food. They could eat it anywhere, without the rules about where holy food had to be eaten. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-18.html

**v. 32**
- Gill says "defiling" the holy things would mean eating from the tithe before giving the priests their tenth. Such neglect was apparently punishable by death. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-18.html

## 2. Where Protestant teachers differ: vv. 21–28 and tithing today

The real split is whether these verses bind Christians to give 10%. The split runs inside traditions, not cleanly between them.

- **Baptist, "not required":** Tom Schreiner says Christians are no longer under the Mosaic covenant. The tithes went to Levites and priests, and there are none under the new covenant. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/7-reasons-christians-not-required-to-tithe/
- **Baptist (Desiring God), "not required":** citing v. 21, the answer given is that since that system of Levitical ministry is now gone, I think the designed support for it is gone. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/can-a-church-require-tithing
- **Presbyterian (PCA), "required":** William Barcley argues tithing came before Moses, was written into the law with ceremonial parts added, and was confirmed by Jesus. He says 10% is the minimum. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/bible-commands-christians-to-tithe/
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** R.C. Sproul calls the tithe the centre of biblical stewardship and urges tithing "from the top". https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/stewardship-tithing-and-giving
- **Calvary Chapel (Enduring Word):** Guzik takes a middle line. The New Testament doesn't command tithing but speaks well of it (Luke 11:42), so 10% is a good goal and not a ceiling. He also mentions the view that the Levitical tithe was really like a tax. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-18/
- **General evangelical (GotQuestions):** Christians are not required to give 10%, but they must support ministry and give in proportion to income. https://www.gotquestions.org/tithing-Christian.html

## 3. Other views

**Modern scholarship (from Precept Austin, which quotes the NET Bible notes and recent commentators)**
- **v. 1:** The NET note says the priests would pay for ritual errors, especially if someone came too near. Because they approached the sanctuary constantly, they were most at risk of breaking its rules. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-18-commentary
- **vv. 1–3:** Ashley and Milgrom set out a chain of responsibility. The priests and Kohathites answer for lay Israelites, the priests for other priests, and priests and Levites together for Levites. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-18-commentary

**Catholic**
- **v. 3:** The Catholic Encyclopedia says Levites could not perform the actual sacrifice, especially sprinkling the blood. That was the priests' privilege. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/12409a.htm
- **v. 21:** The Catholic Encyclopedia says tithes were owed to God, who passed them to his ministers. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/14741b.htm
- **vv. 21, 23–24:** Thomas Aquinas cites v. 21 and argues the clergy are the successors of the sons of Levi in the New Testament. Therefore tithes are due to the clergy alone. He also discusses vv. 26–28 on whether clergy must pay tithes themselves. https://www.newadvent.org/summa/3087.htm
- **vv. 21–24:** Cyprian says the Levites' freedom from land is the pattern for clergy, so they are not tied down by worldly cares. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/050665.htm
- **Today:** The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that compulsory tithing has long since almost everywhere ceased, though the faithful must still support their clergy. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/14296a.htm

**Popular modern teaching**
- I found no prosperity or word-of-faith teaching on this chapter itself, only critics touching on it. Sproul notes that some unscrupulous televangelists have given tithing a bad name. https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/stewardship-tithing-and-giving
- Even Barcley, who argues tithing is required, says God doesn't promise to make you rich, but he will provide your needs. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/bible-commands-christians-to-tithe/
- GotQuestions warns that using Malachi 3's "storehouse" for church giving takes it out of context. https://www.gotquestions.org/Malachi-tithing.html

## What I couldn't find
- No Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist or Wesleyan, or Pentecostal-denominational (ag.org) pages on this chapter.
- No Orthodox (oca.org) material, and nothing from bibleodyssey.org.
- No netbible.org page directly; the NET notes above come only through Precept Austin.
- No hyper-grace teaching.
- The Matthew Henry page came back empty when I opened it. His two points above come only from the search preview.
- The Enduring Word and Precept Austin pages cut off partway. Their notes on vv. 25–32 and vv. 8–32 respectively are thinner than they may actually be.
